title: Medusa
description: A poem from The World's Wife (1999) in which Medusa speaks in the first person about the jealousy that turned her hair to snakes and her eyes to stone, and about the love that keeps her dangerous.
plot_or_argument: Medusa begins with the origin of her condition: 'A suspicion, a doubt, a jealousy / grew in my mind, / which turned the hairs on my head / to filthy snakes / as though my thoughts / hissed and spat on my scalp.' The poem follows the transformation through her body - her breath souring, her lungs 'grey bags', her mouth foul, her teeth yellow fangs, 'bullet tears' in her eyes - and then turns to the man she loves: 'Be terrified. / It's you I love, / perfect man, Greek God, my own; / but I know you'll go, betray me, stray / from home.' She imagines the women he will look at, and what will become of them; she tells him that she is not the monster he thinks, that the stone is the hardening of a love that has been hurt. The poem's final movement is a warning and a confession: the gaze that petrifies is the gaze of someone who has been betrayed and will not be looked at again, and the poem's bitterness is directed as much at the woman's own jealousy as at the man.
narrative_structure: Seven stanzas of free verse, the first of five lines and the rest of six, without a regular rhyme scheme but with strong internal rhyme, assonance and consonance; the poem moves from diagnosis to transformation to address to warning, and ends on an image rather than a statement.
meter_and_prosody: Blunt, monosyllabic, deliberately ugly diction in the transformation stanzas ('foul mouthed', 'yellow fanged') set against the plain tenderness of 'It's you I love'; heavy alliteration and sibilance; short lines and hard enjambments; the tone is jeering, wounded and seductive at once.
historical_context: The World's Wife (Picador, 1999) is Duffy's best-selling collection, a series of dramatic monologues in which the wives and women of myth, history and literature answer back; 'Medusa' belongs to its sequence of classical and biblical retellings, and the collection was written in the years before Duffy became Poet Laureate in 2009.
literary_significance: One of the most widely taught poems of The World's Wife and a standard example of the feminist revisionary myth poem; it is one of Duffy's four selections in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The World's Wife (London: Picador, 1999). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning at page 1160.
thematic_analysis: Duffy rewrites the Medusa myth as the story of a woman destroyed by jealousy rather than by a curse: the snakes are her thoughts, and the petrifying gaze is the hardening of love into suspicion. The poem belongs to The World's Wife's project of giving the women of myth and history their own voices, and it makes a feminist argument about the way women are turned into monsters by the fear of betrayal, while refusing to excuse the violence that Medusa's own suspicion produces. The direct address to the lover makes the poem a love poem as well as a curse, and the imagery of the body - breath, lungs, eyes, teeth - keeps the myth physical.
summary: A dramatic monologue in seven stanzas of free verse, in which Medusa describes her transformation, addresses the man she loves, and warns him - and the reader - not to look at her.
research_notes: The poem's opening and several lines were read through the annotation page cited, which prints the text and describes the seven-stanza structure; it was not read complete from the printed collection.

title: Mrs Lazarus
description: A poem from The World's Wife (1999) in which the wife of Lazarus describes her grief, her slow recovery and remarriage, and the ruin brought back when her husband is raised from the dead.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins in the extremity of grief: Mrs Lazarus shrieks, tears her hair, lies on the grave, and performs the mourning that is expected of her, 'howling' and 'shrieking' until she has no voice left. Then the poem's time begins to move: she takes off her black, goes back to work, learns to sleep alone, and eventually meets another man and marries him. Duffy compresses the years - 'I would have to ask / how long' - and shows the recovery as unspectacular and physical: the body's habits changing, the house rearranged. The last two stanzas bring the miracle: Lazarus returns, and his wife, who has grieved him properly and buried him and made a life, is left with a husband she no longer knows and a new husband she cannot keep. The poem's final image is of the two men and the woman between them, and of 'the hours I had' - the life she had built - being taken back.
narrative_structure: Eight five-line stanzas of free verse, with no rhyme scheme; the poem is chronological, moving from the death to the mourning to the remarriage to the return, and its stanzas shorten and quicken as the miracle approaches.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, first-person, colloquial free verse with a strong physical vocabulary (shrieking, howling, the taste of ash, the smell of the grave); short sentences and abrupt line breaks; a tone that moves from raw grief to domestic calm to a final, quiet horror.
historical_context: The World's Wife (Picador, 1999) reworks the stories of women attached to famous men, from Mrs Midas to Mrs Darwin and Queen Herod; 'Mrs Lazarus' takes the raising of Lazarus in the Gospel of John (11:1-44) as its source and extends the four days of the biblical narrative into years, so that the wife's remarriage becomes credible.
literary_significance: One of the most frequently taught poems of The World's Wife and a set text in British schools; it is one of Duffy's four selections in the Norton Anthology and the collection's clearest example of its method of giving the untold woman's side of a familiar story.
bibliographical_notes: Published in The World's Wife (London: Picador, 1999). A selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, 11th edition, vol. F, beginning at page 1161.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the work of mourning and the way a miracle can be a catastrophe: Lazarus's resurrection, which the Gospel treats as a sign of divine power, is experienced by his wife as the destruction of the life she has slowly rebuilt. Duffy gives the woman the time the biblical narrative does not - the years of widowhood, the second marriage - and makes her grief a process with stages rather than a tableau. The poem is also about the social performance of mourning: the shrieking and hair-tearing that begin it are what is expected, and the poem's interest is in what comes after the performance ends.
summary: A dramatic monologue in eight five-line stanzas of free verse, in which Mrs Lazarus moves from frenzied mourning through the routines of widowhood to a new life, and then confronts the returned Lazarus.
research_notes: The account follows the annotation page cited, which prints the poem's opening stanzas and describes its eight-stanza structure and its departure from the Gospel narrative; the poem was not read complete from the printed collection.

title: Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard
description: An extract from Kiran Desai's first novel, Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard (1998), in which Sampath Chawla, a clerk who has climbed a guava tree in a Shahkot orchard, is discovered there and turned by his family and the town into a holy man.
plot_or_argument: Sampath Chawla, the son of Mr and Mrs Chawla of Shahkot, has failed at school, at his job in the post office and at the marriage his parents arranged for him, and has run away to live in a guava tree in a ruined orchard on the edge of town. The family finds him there: 'Searching for Sampath, the family clacked about the trees and shouted up into the leaves, the three women uttering his name with mournful wails, Mr Chawla shouting like an Army major.' A doctor is consulted and a debate follows over whether Sampath is mad - 'Is he biting his neighbors? Biting himself? Is he sleepwalking? Does he stick out his tongue and roll his eyes? Is he rude to strangers?' - and the answer, that he eats and sleeps and is polite, settles that he is not. The orchard, however, has other visitors: the townspeople, hearing of the man in the tree, begin to bring offerings; and the extract follows the first pilgrims, the gifts of food and money, the raising of a cot and an umbrella into the branches, and the transformation of a failed clerk into a guru whose answers - nonsense delivered with the authority of revelation - become 'the sermon in the guava tree'. The extract ends with Sampath installed in comfort, and with the town's credulity and his family's enterprise in full flood.
narrative_structure: A novel in thirty-odd short chapters, comic and episodic, with a large cast and a narrator who moves between the family's perspective and the town's; the Norton extract is a continuous sequence from the middle of the novel, covering the search, the diagnosis and the first devotees.
meter_and_prosody: Exuberant, comic, over-heated prose with long lists, exclamations and sudden lyric passages; a strong sense of place (the orchard, the town, the railway) and a taste for the absurd; dialogue in an Indian English with a vivid demotic energy, and a narrator who shares the characters' excitability.
historical_context: Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard was published by Faber and Faber in 1998 and won the Betty Trask Award; it was begun while Desai was studying creative writing in the United States, and it draws on her childhood in India and on the tradition of Indian comic fiction. 'The Sermon in the Guava Tree' was printed in The New Yorker in June 1997 as an extract from the then forthcoming novel, and the Norton Anthology reprints a passage of the same material.
literary_significance: Desai's first novel and the book that made her name before The Inheritance of Loss won the Booker Prize in 2006; the guava-tree episode is the novel's central comic idea, and the extract is her selection in the Norton Anthology.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Faber and Faber (London) in 1998. Norton prints an extract under the title 'The Sermon in the Guava Tree', beginning at page 1200; a version of the same material appeared under that title in The New Yorker, 23 June 1997. This record covers the whole novel.
thematic_analysis: Desai's comedy is about the manufacture of sanctity: Sampath is a holy man because he is sitting in a tree and because a town needs a holy man, and the novel's satire is directed at the commercial and religious appetite that produces him. The orchard is also an ecological subject - a remnant of greenery that the town's traffic, rubbish and advertisements gradually overrun - and Sampath's retreat into it is a retreat from the noise of post-independence India into a silence he cannot keep. The family's eagerness to profit from his new status, and the bureaucracy's attempt to manage it, make the novel a study of how private eccentricity is converted into public property.
summary: A comic sequence from the novel: the Chawla family's search for Sampath, the discovery of him in the tree, the debate over whether he is mad, the arrival of the first devotees, and the beginnings of the 'sermon in the guava tree' that makes him a celebrity.
research_notes: The plot of the extract follows the New Yorker text (its opening and the quoted exchanges) and the summaries of the novel in the scholarly and reference sources cited; Desai's own date of first publication for the novel (1998) and the extract's New Yorker appearance (June 1997) are taken from those pages. The novel was not read complete.
